out: Name the files in a domain pack and what each one holds.
Explain how modules, weeks, sessions and lessons fit together.
Explain why the product design layer is kept apart from the domain lessons.
plain: A domain pack is a recipe book with a fixed layout. Every recipe has the same sections in the same order, so a reader always knows where to find the ingredients, and a cook can check a new recipe against the layout before it goes in the book.
tech: A pack lives in domains/<id>/. domain.json holds the title, status, areas (broad parts of the field, which can match an exam's domains), objectives (the specific things learners should be able to do), modules, weeks and the order of sessions in each week. references.json lists every source with its URL, whether it is free, and when it was last opened. Lesson files (*.txt) hold the lessons, questions and labs. The design/ folder holds one design block per lesson, plus any case studies.

Learners see modules, which group weeks, and weeks, which list sessions in order: lessons, reviews and case studies. A lesson has outcomes, a plain-language explanation, technical detail, terms, examples, a walkthrough, a lab, a scenario, questions, common mistakes, a summary, flashcards and references. The build script, scripts/build-domains.py, refuses to publish a lesson that is missing any of these.

The design layer is stored separately so that design writing can never make domain knowledge look covered. Each lesson is marked direct (a full design exercise), professional (questions to ask engineering, security and product, with no exercise) or foundation (why it matters, with no exercise).
terms: One field of study, organized as a folder that the build script turns into a course.
A broad part of a field, such as threats or architecture.
A specific thing a learner should be able to do, used to map questions and lessons.
One item in a week: a lesson, a review or a case study.
The part of each lesson that applies the domain to product design work.
eg: The security domain has 13 weeks in seven modules. Week 7 lists six lessons, then a review. Each lesson file holds several lessons, and design/d1-w01-07.txt holds their design blocks.

Direct (a full exercise), professional (stakeholder questions) and foundation (why it matters).
lessons.title: What a domain pack is, and how learners move through it
lessons.why: A domain pack turns one field, such as security or healthcare, into a course designers can follow. If you know the shape before you write, every lesson you add slots into a path that already works: the app, the checks and the progress tracking need no changes.
lessons.scenario: A healthcare expert wants to add a domain. They have written 20 lessons in a document, each with an explanation and some quiz questions, but no labs, walkthroughs or design notes. What will happen when they try to build it, and what should they do first?
lessons.answer: The build will refuse every lesson, because labs, walkthroughs and design blocks are required. They should first write domain.json with the weeks and objectives, convert one lesson fully, get it through the build and an expert review, and use it as the model for the rest.

product: A predictable lesson shape is itself a design decision: learners always know where the example, the lab and the questions are, which lowers effort and makes progress easy to see.
design.noex: This lesson describes the format; the next lessons in any domain apply it.

out: Write a lesson block that passes the automated checks.
Write questions whose options each carry a clear explanation.
Explain how AI drafting, references and expert review keep a domain trustworthy.
plain: The build script is a spell checker for structure: it notices a missing section the way a spell checker notices a typo. An expert reviewer is an editor who knows the subject: they notice when a sentence is perfectly formed and simply wrong.
tech: Each lesson starts with @lesson and an id, followed by one key per line, such as title:, obj:, level:, out:, plain: and tech:. Questions start with q, then the objective, the kind (mcq, multi, tf, order or match) and the difficulty (e, m or h), then the concept and the question. Each option starts with + for right or - for wrong, followed by :: and the reason. Multiple choice needs exactly four options and one right answer. Ordering and matching questions need a why: line.

Every reference must be listed in references.json with a URL, marked free, and with the date someone last opened it. A link that has not been opened is not added. Lessons may be drafted with AI, but the draft must say so in the pull request, and a domain expert must review it before it is merged. Reviewers check facts, emphasis and examples, not just wording.

Write plainly. Prefer short sentences, define every acronym the first time, and give one concrete example for each idea. Put the commonly confused pair in a table. Explain why each wrong option is wrong, because that is where most learning happens.
terms: The lines from @lesson to the next @lesson, holding one complete lesson.
The reason after :: that says why an option is right or wrong.
A check by someone who works in the field, focused on accuracy and emphasis.
Saying in the pull request that a draft was written with an AI model.
eg: A question with three options fails the build with: multiple choice needs four options. Adding a plausible fourth option, with its reason, fixes it.
A reviewer notices that a lesson calls a technique outdated when it is still recommended. The build could never catch this; the review did.

walks.title: Take one lesson from draft to merged
steps: Copy a lesson block from an existing domain as a starting point.
Replace the content, keeping every key, and add the design block in design/.
Add any new sources to references.json, after opening each one.
Run the build and fix every problem it lists.
Open a pull request, say whether AI was used, and ask a domain expert to review.
Make the reviewer's changes, then the lesson can be merged.

Run: python3 scripts/build-domains.py authoring and read the problem it reports.

lessons.title: Writing a lesson that passes the checks and expert review
lessons.why: Learners act on what they read, and hiring managers judge designers by what they learned. A domain is only as good as its least accurate lesson. The format and the checks catch missing parts; people catch wrong facts. This lesson shows how to give both the best chance.
lessons.scenario: A contributor submits ten lessons drafted with AI in one afternoon. All ten pass the build. The pull request does not mention AI, and no expert has reviewed it. What should the maintainer do?
lessons.answer: Ask the contributor to disclose how the drafts were made, and hold the merge until a domain expert has reviewed each lesson. Passing the build proves the structure is complete, not that the facts are right. Suggest splitting the work into smaller pull requests, so a reviewer can check each lesson properly.

product: Every domain is an information product that people act on. The review workflow is part of its user experience: it decides how quickly errors are found, and how much learners can trust what they read.

eng: Can the build run on every pull request, so contributors see problems before review?
sec: How are contributions checked for copied or unlicensed material?
prod: How do learners report an error, and how quickly is it fixed?
